sections.content: You already met 'miután' (after) and 'mielőtt' (before) earlier — these subordinate conjunctions link two past events by saying which one happened first. Now you'll use them for real: to explain WHY the Magyar tribes left the steppe. Unlike English, Hungarian keeps the same past tense in both clauses — there's no separate 'had done' form to worry about.

sections.title: miután vs. mielőtt
rows: the Pechenegs, the Khazars (this lesson's key peoples)

items.spanish: Miután a besenyők egyre nagyobb nyomást gyakoroltak rájuk, a magyar törzsek elhagyták Etelközt.
items.english: After the Pechenegs put increasing pressure on them, the Magyar tribes abandoned Etelköz.

items.spanish: Mielőtt a magyarok véglegesen elindultak nyugatra, sokáig próbálták megtartani keleti szállásaikat.
items.english: Before the Magyars finally set out west, they tried for a long time to hold on to their eastern territory.

items.spanish: A kazárok, miután maguk is meggyengültek, már nem tudták megvédeni szövetségeseiket.
items.english: The Khazars, after they themselves had weakened, could no longer protect their allies.

sections.content: The clause with 'miután'/'mielőtt' can come first or second in the sentence — word order is flexible, but when it comes first, put a comma before the main clause. Notice that Hungarian never needs a pluperfect ('had weakened') the way English does: 'miután meggyengültek' already makes clear that the weakening came first, just from the conjunction itself.
